record.paper_title: Enabling and Emerging Technologies for Social Distancing: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can GNSS-based social distancing services that track users, monitor groups, keep people apart, and collect infected-movement data achieve reliable accuracy for distances below two meters without relying on expensive or sparsely deployed advanced GNSS infrastructure, while also protecting location and identity privacy?

evidence.quote: Furthermore, in terms of determining the distance between two people, the accuracy of GNSS services is not high in general, especially for distances less than two meters.

Thus, some recent advanced GNSS technologies like [146], [148], [149], [155] can be used to improve the accuracy of the GPS. However, these technologies are still quite expensive and have not been widely deployed for public services, and thus more research in this direction should be further explored. For the privacy issues, they will be discussed in Section V with several solutions such as location information protection and personal identity protection.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a system in which a population of users carry mobile devices equipped with standard Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers. The system is required to provide four social-distancing services: (i) continuously tracking each user's position, (ii) monitoring the formation of groups (clusters of users in close spatial proximity), (iii) issuing alerts when any two users come within a threshold distance d < 2 meters of each other, and (iv) recording the movement trajectories of users identified as infected. Standard consumer GNSS positioning has horizontal error typically on the order of several meters, which is insufficient to reliably resolve pairwise distances below 2 meters. Advanced GNSS augmentation techniques (e.g., real-time kinematic positioning, precise point positioning, multi-constellation differential corrections, and dense reference-station networks) can in principle achieve sub-meter or centimeter-level accuracy, but they require costly hardware and infrastructure that is not widely deployed for public use.

Design a GNSS-based social-distancing protocol and prove its correctness with respect to the following requirements:

1. (Accuracy) Using only commodity GNSS receivers and publicly available signals — without relying on dense networks of differential reference stations or other expensive, sparsely deployed augmentation infrastructure — the protocol must reliably determine the pairwise distance between any two users with sufficient accuracy to decide whether they are within a threshold d < 2 meters, with provable bounds on false-positive and false-negative rates under realistic GNSS error models (multipath, atmospheric delays, receiver noise).

2. (Location privacy) The protocol must not reveal any user's absolute or relative location to the service provider or to other users, beyond what is strictly necessary to issue proximity alerts and to record infected-user trajectories.

3. (Identity privacy) The protocol must not reveal the identity of any user (including infected users whose movements are recorded) to other users or to unauthorized parties.

Either construct such a protocol together with formal accuracy and privacy guarantees, or prove that no such protocol exists under stated assumptions on GNSS error and adversary models.
artifact.status_search_result: No published work was located that fully resolves the combined challenge of achieving sub-two-meter GNSS-based proximity detection with commodity receivers while simultaneously providing rigorous location and identity privacy guarantees. Research on RTK/PPP and on privacy-preserving contact tracing has progressed separately, but the joint problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Enabling and Emerging Technologies for Social Distancing (survey)
status_evidence.snippet: Notes that GNSS accuracy is generally insufficient for distances below two meters and that advanced GNSS technologies remain expensive and not widely deployed; lists this as an open research direction.
status_evidence.claim: The combined accuracy-and-privacy GNSS social-distancing problem is identified as an open challenge.
